source.title: A Mathematical Theory for Learning Semantic Languages by Abstract Learners
source.authors: Kuo-Yu Liao; Cheng-Shang Chang; Y. Hong

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses scaling laws and derives its own results for abstract learners, but it does not test the stated language-model loss, extrapolation, allocation, architecture, modality, or downstream-performance claims.
record.gate_note: The paper derives testing-error results for abstract learners, not held-out cross-entropy loss for language models. Its theoretical error curves and thresholds therefore do not measure any listed claim version. The paper also notes that its scaling law concerns training-text size and that parameter-count scaling remains unclear; this is not a test of the listed versions.
record.test_reason: Purely theoretical density-evolution analysis of abstract skill-text graph learners. It trains no language models and measures no held-out loss. Its 'scaling law' is a testing-error curve versus the ratio of training texts to skills, with threshold (phase-transition) behaviour, not a power law in parameters, tokens or compute. It mentions Kaplan and Hoffmann only as motivation, so it neither tests nor uses V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors derive a density-evolution theory of skill emergence in abstract learners, including thresholds and a testing-error scaling law in the text-to-skill ratio. They acknowledge large gaps from real LLMs, including unclear parameter-count scaling, and leave experimental verification for future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives results for abstract skill-text graph learners using density evolution; it does not run language-model scaling experiments or measure cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported thresholds vary with learner type and the average number of skills per text. For the domain-specific setting, the testing error depends on both the basic-text ratio R and domain-specific-text ratio Rf.

fits_no_version.finding: In abstract 1-skill and 2-skill learners on random skill-text bipartite graphs, testing error drops sharply once the text-to-skill ratio R passes a threshold. The threshold depends on c: about 1, 1.5 and 2.5 for c=3, 4 and 5 (1-skill); about 0.5 and 0.6 for c=4 and 5 (2-skill). The hierarchical fine-tuning setting shows two thresholds, in R and in Rf.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Theoretical skill-graph models predict threshold-like (emergent) drops in testing error with training-data-to-skill ratio.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications
record.problems: The paper explicitly identifies a gap between its abstract learners and real transformer-based language models, says it is unclear how testing error scales with parameter count, and describes real-world experimental verification as difficult. Its analysis relies on Poisson degree and uniform-connection assumptions. It also notes discrepancies between theory and simulation for the skill-association analysis at c=1 and c=2.

untested.parts: All: no language-model held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
All: the foundation-model plus fine-tuning hierarchy is abstract, with no loss power law in real systems.
All: no downstream task measurements of real models.
All: no fitted exponents or comparison of fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly linked to none and correctly marked cannot_determine. The study also contains giant-component and multi-class results (Figures 7–9 and 13), which likewise bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss and power-law dependence on parameters, tokens, or compute in language models.
Whether fits on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as a function of compute.
Effects of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream-task performance and its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.
